title: The Essence and the Energies, in the Words of the Fathers
subtitle: A florilegium of patristic and Scriptural witnesses
source: A florilegium gathered with a Purify reader (Discord: ChristosAnesti). Each Father's words are given word for word from the public-domain English of the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, read from CCEL's transcription of each volume, and Scripture from the Bible Purify reads (Brenton's Septuagint for the Old Testament, the King James Version for the New). Where a Father's words have no public-domain English, his teaching is told in our words and marked as ours. The framing is by the editors of Purify.

sections.title: The doctrine in one sentence
paragraphs: God's essence is unknowable to every creature. His energies are God Himself as known, encountered, communicated. To partake of God is to partake of the uncreated energies; the essence remains forever beyond participation. Theosis, the deification of the saints, is real because the energies through which God acts in the world are truly God, not a creature.

Behind this short sentence stand many centuries of patristic teaching. The grammar by which the Church speaks of God being one and yet truly participated, transcendent and yet truly immanent, was hammered out by the Cappadocians against Eunomius in the fourth century, refined by Cyril of Alexandria and Maximus the Confessor in the fifth and seventh, and given its mature dogmatic formulation by Gregory Palamas and the Constantinopolitan synods of 1341, 1347, and 1351 against Barlaam, Akindynos, and the later Latinizers.
notes: There is a live academic discussion about the precise modal grammar of the Palamite distinction, whether it is best read as a real distinction in the late Scholastic sense, as a formal distinction, or as something the East has its own categories for. Tikhon Pino's *Essence and Energies* (2023), in Palamas's licensed works on this profile, lays out the current scholarship; we name the question here and do not pronounce a judgment beyond the patristic witnesses themselves.

This page is a florilegium, a gathering of flowers from the wider patristic garden. It is not a translation of any one work. Each Father's words below are given word for word from the public-domain English named with them; where none exists, his teaching is told in our words and marked so.

sections.title: Scripture's witness to the divine operations
sections.framing: The Name God gives to Moses at the burning bush, which St. Athanasius reads as the intimation of an incomprehensible essence, and the Apostle's words for God's working. The passages give one rule: God is known not by direct vision of the essence but through the works that are His. St. Paul uses the Greek word energeia (energy, working, operation) as a real and concrete name for the activity of God in the Church and in creation.
sections.citation: Exodus 3:14 in Brenton's Septuagint; Romans 1:20, John 10:38, Ephesians 1:19-20, Philippians 3:21 and 1 Corinthians 12:11 in the King James Version
paragraphs: Exodus 3:14. And God spoke to Moses, saying, I am THE BEING; and he said, Thus shall ye say to the children of Israel, THE BEING has sent me to you.

Romans 1:20. For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
John 10:38. But if I do, though ye believe not me, believe the works: that ye may know, and believe, that the Father is in me, and I in him.

Ephesians 1:19-20. And what is the exceeding greatness of his power to us-ward who believe, according to the working of his mighty power, Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places,
Philippians 3:21. Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself.
1 Corinthians 12:11. But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.
notes: St. John Chrysostom, expounding 1 Corinthians, takes the diverse 'workings' (*energeiai*) of the Spirit as the one divine action of God Himself in its many manifestations, the same grammar Palamas inherits and clarifies a thousand years later.

sections.title: The essence is incomprehensible: St. Cyril of Jerusalem
sections.framing: In his sixth Catechetical Lecture, on the Unity of God, St. Cyril asks whether a creature can comprehend the divine nature, when even the throne the prophet describes is beyond understanding.
sections.citation: Catechetical Lectures VI.3, in NPNF Series II Vol. 7 (1894)
paragraphs: But if we cannot understand the throne, which he has described, how shall we be able to comprehend Him who sitteth thereon, the Invisible and Ineffable God? To scrutinise then the nature of God is impossible: but it is in our power to send up praises of His glory for His works that are seen.
notes: The contributor labelled this passage Catechetical Lectures 2 to 3 in the original submission. It stands in Catechesis VI, on the Unity of God, section 3.

sections.title: The essence is incomprehensible: St. Athanasius
sections.framing: St. Athanasius, defending the words of the Council of Nicaea, on what Scripture's names for God signify.
sections.citation: Defence of the Nicene Definition 22, in NPNF Series II Vol. 4 (1892)
paragraphs: For though to comprehend what the essence of God is be impossible, yet if we only understand that God is, and if Scripture indicates Him by means of these titles, we, with the intention of indicating Him and none else, call Him God and Father and Lord. When then He says, ‘I am that I am,’ and ‘I am the Lord God,’ or when Scripture says, ‘God,’ we understand nothing else by it but the intimation of His incomprehensible essence Itself, and that He Is, who is spoken of.

sections.title: The essence is incomprehensible: St. John Chrysostom
sections.framing: St. John Chrysostom, opening his second homily on the Epistle to the Hebrews.
sections.citation: Homilies on Hebrews II.1, in NPNF Series I Vol. 14 (1889)
paragraphs: For many of our conceptions about God, we are unable to express, as also many things we express, but have not strength to conceive of them. As for instance:—That God is everywhere, we know; but how, we no longer understand. That there is a certain incorporeal power the cause of all our good things, we know: but how it is, or what it is, we know not. Lo! we speak, and do not understand.
notes: Chrysostom's longer treatment of the same theme is his five homilies *On the Incomprehensible Nature of God*, preached at Antioch around 386 against the Eunomian claim that God's essence is fully accessible to reason.

sections.title: God known through His operations: St. Basil the Great
sections.framing: St. Basil, answering those who would not give the Holy Spirit the name of God, on how the divine nature is known.
sections.citation: Letter 189.6, to Eustathius the physician, in NPNF Series II Vol. 8 (1895)
paragraphs: But the divine nature is too exalted to be perceived as objects of enquiry are perceived, and about things which are beyond our knowledge we reason on probable evidence. We are therefore of necessity guided in the investigation of the divine nature by its operations. Suppose we observe the operations of the Father, of the Son, of the Holy Ghost, to be different from one another, we shall then conjecture, from the diversity of the operations that the operating natures are also different. For it is impossible that things which are distinct, as regards their nature, should be associated as regards the form of their operations; fire does not freeze; ice does not warm; difference of natures implies difference of the operations proceeding from them. Grant, then, that we perceive the operation of Father, Son and Holy Ghost to be one and the same, in no respect showing difference or variation; from this identity of operation we necessarily infer the unity of the nature.
notes: St. Basil's argument in Letter 189 is one of the foundational passages for the patristic doctrine of the one divine operation. The Eastern Fathers will read his identity-of-operation argument as already presupposing the essence-and-energies grammar that Palamas later names explicitly.

sections.title: God known through His operations: St. John Chrysostom
sections.framing: St. John Chrysostom, on the opening words of St. John's Gospel.
sections.citation: Homilies on John II.8, in NPNF Series I Vol. 14 (1889)
paragraphs: our argument is God, whom it is impossible to describe, or to imagine worthily; hence this man nowhere assigns the name of His essence, (for it is not possible to say what God is, as to essence,) but everywhere he declares Him to us by His workings. For this “Word” one may see shortly after called “Light,” and the “Light” in turn named “Life.”

sections.title: God known through His operations: St. Ambrose of Milan
sections.framing: St. Ambrose, teaching the newly baptized, on the same words of St. Paul.
sections.citation: On the Mysteries 8, in NPNF Series II Vol. 10 (1896)
paragraphs: For you read elsewhere: “That the invisible things of God, since the creation of the world, are understood through those things which have been made; His eternal power also and Godhead are estimated by His works.” Wherefore also the Lord Himself says: “If ye believe not Me, believe at least the works.” Believe, then, that the presence of the Godhead is there. Do you believe the working, and not believe the presence? Whence should the working proceed unless the presence went before?
notes: Ambrose's *cognoscuntur* in the Latin ('are known by His works') runs parallel to the Eastern grammar of *energeiai* exactly. The doctrine is not exclusively Eastern in its patristic ground.

sections.title: The Transfiguration: the uncreated light on Tabor
paragraphs: The Tabor light is not a created splendour added to Christ's humanity from outside; it is the eternal glory of the Word, made visible to the disciples as their eyes are made able to bear it. This is the patristic ground on which Palamas later rests his case that the saints' vision of God is a vision of the uncreated.

St. Ephraim the Syrian's homily on the Transfiguration, which has no public-domain English, is told in our words on his page: on the mountain the disciples saw the glory of the divinity that His humanity had hidden, His face bright as lightning and His garments white as light.
notes: St. Gregory Palamas, in the Hagiorite Tome (1340), makes the Tabor light the test case for the doctrine: if the light is created, theosis is participation in a creature; if it is uncreated, theosis is real participation in God.

sections.title: Operation: St. John of Damascus
sections.framing: St. John of Damascus, on the two energies of Christ, gives the grammar of operation that St. Gregory Palamas inherits.
sections.citation: An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith III.15, in NPNF Series II Vol. 9 (1899)
paragraphs: We hold, further, that there are two energies in our Lord Jesus Christ. For He possesses on the one hand, as God and being of like essence with the Father, the divine energy, and, likewise, since He became man and of like essence to us, the energy proper to human nature.

But observe that energy and capacity for energy, and the product of energy, and the agent of energy, are all different. Energy is the efficient (δραστική) and essential activity of nature: the capacity for energy is the nature from which proceeds energy: the product of energy is that which is effected by energy: and the agent of energy is the person or subsistence which uses the energy.
notes: John of Damascus's fourfold grammar (energy / capacity for energy / product of energy / agent of energy) is the technical lexicon Palamas inherits. The seventh-century clarification against monothelitism (one will or two?) is the immediate background.

The same Damascene passage names energy as 'the efficacious and substantial motion of the nature' (ἡ δραστικὴ καὶ οὐσιώδης τῆς φύσεως κίνησις), which is the formula Palamas cites repeatedly in the 150 Chapters.
St. Maximus the Confessor's Chapters on Theology, which the first gathering quoted beside this passage, have no public-domain English, so they are left out.

sections.title: Cyril of Alexandria against created energies
paragraphs: St. Cyril of Alexandria, in the *Dialogues on the Trinity* Book VII (PG 75, 1109 B-C), argues that the divine operation cannot be a creature. If anyone says that the Spirit, that is, the operation by which God works in creation, is itself a creature, then since God's operation is no other thing than He Himself, God Himself would be a creature, an abominable conclusion.

Cyril's principle: the divine being is simple and incomposite; it is not composed of nature and energy as though these were naturally other in the divine; the energy of God is God Himself proper to Him. To call the operation a creature is to call God a creature.
notes: The English text submitted by the contributor was drawn from the modern Boulnois / de Durand French and English critical editions of the *Dialogues on the Trinity*, which are under copyright. The summary above paraphrases the same passage from the standard reference (PG 75, 1109 B–C) in our own words. Readers who want the precise modern translation should consult the published edition.

Cyril's argument (that no created intermediary can mediate God to creation, because God's energy is God Himself) is the patristic foundation against any later view (Akindynos, the early Barlaam) that the divine grace given to the saints is a creature.

sections.title: Palamas: identical and distinct
paragraphs: In the One Hundred and Fifty Chapters St. Gregory Palamas teaches that the divine energy is neither God's essence nor an accident in Him. An accident comes into being and passes away, and nothing in the unchanging God does; yet not everything said of God names His essence, for some things are said of Him in relation to something else, and the divine energy is of that kind: it is in God, and it is not His essence (Chapter 135).
The three divine Persons, he teaches, have one energy: not one by likeness, as several men share one kind of work, but truly and numerically one (Chapter 138).

God's essence has no name of its own, since it is wholly beyond comprehension; it is named, not properly, from all its energies, and every such name points to the one Hidden God. The energies, by contrast, are each named by what God does: creating, ruling, judging, providing, and adopting us as sons by grace are different from one another (Chapter 144).

In his letters to Daniel of Ainos and to Gabras he gathers this into one rule from the Fathers: in one sense essence and energy are the same in God and in another they differ, and the mind distinguishes them for our sake without dividing or separating what is indivisible.
notes: No public-domain English of St. Gregory Palamas's writings has been found, so his teaching is told here in our words, with the chapters it comes from. The quotations the first gathering gave were from modern translations still in copyright.

These four teachings are the spine of the mature Palamite doctrine: the energies are neither accidents nor creatures; they are truly and numerically one in the three Persons; they bear distinct names for what God does, while the essence has no proper name of its own; and the distinction is real and indivisible at once. Pino's 2023 volume, on this profile's Licensed Works shelf, walks through these passages with care.
